sections.normalized_html:
The linear model that estimates the fish population, [MATH: F(t),] in thousands, for [MATH: t] years after [MATH: 2000,] is

[MATH: F(t) = mt + b.]

We have two known data points:

[MATH: (t_{1}, y_{1})|= (0, 220); (t_{2}, y_{2})|= (15, 400)]

First, we calculate the slope [MATH: m{:}]

[MATH: m|= (y_{2} − y_{1})/(x_{2} − x_{1}); = (400 − 220)/(15 − 0); = (180)/(15); = 12]

Then, since the population in [MATH: 2000] (when [MATH: t=0]) is [MATH: 220] thousand fish, we have [MATH: b = 220.] So we get

[MATH: F(t)|= mt + b; = 12t + 220.]

To find the fish population in [MATH: 2008,] we need to substitute into the above expression [MATH: t=8.] Therefore, the population in [MATH: 2008,] in thousands, is

[MATH: y|= F(8); = 12 × 8 + 220; = 96 + 220; = 316.]

sections.normalized_html: A linear function [MATH: h(x)] gives the total cost, in dollars, of producing [MATH: x] custom bicycles. The total cost is [MATH: \[math]720] to produce [MATH: 6] bicycles, and [MATH: \[/math]1,200] to produce [MATH: 12] bicycles. What is the equation that defines [MATH: h(x)?]
sections.readable_text: A linear function [MATH: h(x)] gives the total cost, in dollars, of producing [MATH: x] custom bicycles. The total cost is [MATH: \[math]720] to produce [MATH: 6] bicycles, and [MATH: \[/math]1,200] to produce [MATH: 12] bicycles. What is the equation that defines [MATH: h(x)?]

sections.normalized_html:
The linear function modeling this situation is

[MATH: h(x) = mx + b.]

We know two points on the line:

[MATH: (x_{1}, y_{1})|= (6, 720); (x_{2}, y_{2})|= (12, 1, 200)]

Using the given two points, we find the slope [MATH: m{:}]

[MATH: m|= (y_{2} − y_{1})/(x_{2} − x_{1}); = (1, 200 − 720)/(12 − 6); = (480)/(6); = 80]

So, the linear function is [MATH: h(x)|= mx + b; = 80x + b.]

To find the value of [MATH: b,] we substitute one of the points, say [MATH: (6, 720),] into this equation:

[MATH: 720|= 80 × 6 + b; 720|= 480 + b; b|= 240]

Therefore, the linear equation that defines [MATH: h(x)] is

[MATH: h(x) = 80x + 240.]

sections.normalized_html: An analyst modeled the demand [MATH: Q] for a certain winter coat as a linear function of the selling price [MATH: p.] The demand was [MATH: 24,000] units when the price was [MATH: \[math]150] per unit, and [MATH: 18,000] units when the price was [MATH: \[/math]200] per unit. Based on this model, what is the demand, in units, when the price is [MATH: \[math]180] per unit?

Based on this model, what is the demand, in units, when the price is [MATH: \[math]180] per unit?

sections.normalized_html:
The linear function that models the demand [MATH: Q,] in units, for a selling price [MATH: p,] in dollars, is

[MATH: Q(p) = mp + b.]

We have two known data points:

[MATH: (p_{1}, Q_{1}) = (150, 24, 000); (p_{2}, Q_{2}) = (200, 18, 000)]

We first find the slope [MATH: m{:}]

[MATH: m|= (Q_{2} − Q_{1})/(p_{2} − p_{1}); = (18, 000 − 24, 000)/(200 − 150); = (− 6, 000)/(50); = − 120]

So the demand function is

[MATH: Q(p)|= mp + b; = − 120p + b.]

Now, we use one of the given points, say [MATH: (150, 24,000),] to find the value of [MATH: b{:}]

[MATH: 24, 000|= − 120 × 150 + b; 24, 000|= − 18, 000 + b; b|= 42, 000]

So we have

[MATH: Q(p) = -120p + 42,000.]

To find the demand for the price [MATH: \[math]180] per unit, we need to substitute into the above expression [MATH: p = 180.] This gives

[MATH: Q(180)|= − 120 × 180 + 42, 000; = − 21, 600 + 42, 000; = 20, 400.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
This topic provides more practice in constructing linear functions that model and solve real-world situations. This time, we'll practice using slope-intercept form.

---

Item 2 — Example: Constructing a Linear Function Using Slope-Intercept Form (Intercept Given)

Example Prompt:
A linear model estimates the fish population in a lake from [MATH: 2000] to [MATH: 2015.] The model estimates the population was [MATH: 220] thousand fish in [MATH: 2000,] [MATH: 400] thousand fish in [MATH: 2015,] and [MATH: y] thousand fish in [MATH: 2008.] What is the value of [MATH: y?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The linear model that estimates the fish population, [MATH: F(t),] in thousands, for [MATH: t] years after [MATH: 2000,] is

[MATH: F(t) = mt + b.]

We have two known data points:

[MATH: (t_{1}, y_{1})|= (0, 220); (t_{2}, y_{2})|= (15, 400)]

First, we calculate the slope [MATH: m{:}]

[MATH: m|= (y_{2} − y_{1})/(x_{2} − x_{1}); = (400 − 220)/(15 − 0); = (180)/(15); = 12]

Then, since the population in [MATH: 2000] (when [MATH: t=0]) is [MATH: 220] thousand fish, we have [MATH: b = 220.] So we get

[MATH: F(t)|= mt + b; = 12t + 220.]

To find the fish population in [MATH: 2008,] we need to substitute into the above expression [MATH: t=8.]
Therefore, the population in [MATH: 2008,] in thousands, is

[MATH: y|= F(8); = 12 × 8 + 220; = 96 + 220; = 316.]

Item 5 — Example: Constructing a Linear Function Using Slope-Intercept Form

Example Prompt:
A linear function [MATH: h(x)] gives the total cost, in dollars, of producing [MATH: x] custom bicycles. The total cost is [MATH: \[math]720] to produce [MATH: 6] bicycles, and [MATH: \[/math]1,200] to produce [MATH: 12] bicycles. What is the equation that defines [MATH: h(x)?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The linear function modeling this situation is

[MATH: h(x) = mx + b.]

We know two points on the line:

[MATH: (x_{1}, y_{1})|= (6, 720); (x_{2}, y_{2})|= (12, 1, 200)]

Using the given two points, we find the slope [MATH: m{:}]

[MATH: m|= (y_{2} − y_{1})/(x_{2} − x_{1}); = (1, 200 − 720)/(12 − 6); = (480)/(6); = 80]

So, the linear function is
[MATH: h(x)|= mx + b; = 80x + b.]

To find the value of [MATH: b,] we substitute one of the points, say [MATH: (6, 720),] into this equation:

[MATH: 720|= 80 × 6 + b; 720|= 480 + b; b|= 240]

Therefore, the linear equation that defines [MATH: h(x)] is

[MATH: h(x) = 80x + 240.]

Item 8 — Example: Constructing a Linear Function With a Decreasing Rate

Example Prompt:
The population of pine trees in a forest dropped from [MATH: 9,200] trees in [MATH: 2012] to [MATH: 7,400] trees in [MATH: 2020.] Assuming the population decreased at a constant rate, what is the linear function [MATH: Q(t)] that best models the population, in trees, [MATH: t] years after [MATH: 2012?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The linear function that models the population, [MATH: Q(t),] for [MATH: t] years after [MATH: 2012,] is

[MATH: Q(t)|= mt + b.]

We have two known points:

[MATH: for [math]2012[/math]:(t_{1}, Q_{1})|= (0, 9, 200); for [math]2020[/math]:(t_{2}, Q_{2})|= (8, 7, 400)]

We first find the slope [MATH: m{:}]

[MATH: m|= (Q_{2} − Q_{1})/(t_{2} − t_{1}); = (7, 400 − 9, 200)/(8 − 0); = (− 1, 800)/(8); = − 225]

Then, since the tree population in [MATH: 2012] (when [MATH: t=0]) is [MATH: 9,200,] we have [MATH: b = 9,200.] So we get

[MATH: Q(t)|= mt + b; = − 225t + 9, 200.]

Item 11 — Example: Constructing and Evaluating a Linear Function Using Slope-Intercept Form

Example Prompt:
An analyst modeled the demand [MATH: Q] for a certain winter coat as a linear function of the selling price [MATH: p.] The demand was [MATH: 24,000] units when the price was [MATH: \[math]150] per unit, and [MATH: 18,000] units when the price was [MATH: \[/math]200] per unit. Based on this model, what is the demand, in units, when the price is [MATH: \[math]180] per unit?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The linear function that models the demand [MATH: Q,] in units, for a selling price [MATH: p,] in dollars, is

[MATH: Q(p) = mp + b.]

We have two known data points:

[MATH: (p_{1}, Q_{1}) = (150, 24, 000); (p_{2}, Q_{2}) = (200, 18, 000)]

We first find the slope [MATH: m{:}]

[MATH: m|= (Q_{2} − Q_{1})/(p_{2} − p_{1}); = (18, 000 − 24, 000)/(200 − 150); = (− 6, 000)/(50); = − 120]

So the demand function is

[MATH: Q(p)|= mp + b; = − 120p + b.]

Now, we use one of the given points, say [MATH: (150, 24,000),] to find the value of [MATH: b{:}]

[MATH: 24, 000|= − 120 × 150 + b; 24, 000|= − 18, 000 + b; b|= 42, 000]

So we have

[MATH: Q(p) = -120p + 42,000.]

To find the demand for the price [MATH: \[math]180] per unit, we need to substitute into the above expression [MATH: p = 180.] This gives

[MATH: Q(180)|= − 120 × 180 + 42, 000; = − 21, 600 + 42, 000; = 20, 400.]
